title: Remembering without monuments
hookLine: Sikhs remember the dead through seva and prayer, not monuments
tomorrow: Bebe wants a reading at home. is it for grief, or for thanks?

lines: NO STONE, NO PLOT, NO NAME.
cards: Maya mentions it lightly, over fries after school: on her grandma's birthday her family drives out to the cemetery, brings flowers, and tells her the news. Simran nods, and then it hits her.
There's nowhere like that for Baba. No stone, no plot, no name carved anywhere. The river took everything.
On the bus home she scrolls back through the photos from the porch, the sparrows, the bent wing. Where do you go, she texts Maya, when there's no place?

teach.h: NO STONE AT THE CREMATION PLACE.
teach.b: So, the question: how do you remember someone with no grave? The Sikh answer is with your hands and your voice. The Rehat Maryada asks that no monument be raised where the body was cremated.

Instead, families remember with seva, service, and with prayer: a langar served, a reading held, a job done for someone else in the departed's name. So on Sunday, Simran and Maya stand in the gurdwara kitchen.
Maya's roti comes out shaped like a map of Ohio. Nobody minds. They serve the whole line, in Baba's name.
Now a neighbor, in its own words.

In Islam, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in paraphrase from Sahih Muslim 1631: when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except three: charity that keeps flowing, knowledge that benefits others, and a good child who prays for them.
Muslims call the first sadaqah jariyah. Here's the shared thing, worth telling a friend tonight: both traditions remember the dead with good that keeps going after them.

teach.h: A GRAVE; A RIVER AND A KITCHEN.
teach.b: And the honest difference: Muslims bury their dead, and a grave is there to visit.
Sikhs return the ashes to the water and keep no grave; the remembering is in the kitchen.

how: Sikh families remember the dead without monuments: they sponsor or serve langar, hold a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, give to good causes and do seva in the departed's name, often on the anniversary.

o: remembering the dead with service, not a stone
keeping the departed's room just as it was
building a shrine at the place of cremation

games.q: remembering, two ways — tap the pairs.
p: no monument at the cremation place
a langar served, a job done

s: Sikhs don't remember the dead, because they keep no graves
they remember with seva, langar and prayer in the departed's name.
a hadith names charity that keeps flowing as good that continues after death
Sahih Muslim 1631: charity, beneficial knowledge, a good child who prays.
Muslims and Sikhs mark the dead the same way
shared: good that keeps going. different: Muslims bury and keep a grave; Sikhs return ashes to water.

games.q: your Sikh friend asks how to mark her grandfather's first anniversary. there's no grave. what fits the Sikh way?
o: put up a small memorial plaque at the gurdwara.
serve or sponsor a langar, or hold a reading, in his name.
let the day pass quietly; remembering keeps the grief going.
games.why: no stone, but plenty of remembering: seva, langar and prayer in his name. remember with seva.

practice: Think of someone you've lost, or someone who shaped you.

While the sit runs, do one small thing for someone else in their name: wash a cup that isn't yours, set a coin aside for a good cause, send a kind word to someone who needs it. Say their name to yourself as you do it.

wordCard.voice: Remembering without monuments. Sikhs raise no memorial stone; they remember the dead with seva, langar and prayer in their name.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: seva, selfless service; how Sikhs remember the dead instead of a monument.

carryVoice: Here is the line: remember with seva, a plate served or a cup washed, in their name. Day done.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, Antam Sanskar (no monument at the cremation place), paraphrased
Sahih Muslim 1631 (deeds end at death except three: ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge, a righteous child who prays), paraphrased
